title: Spending fewer tokens can be a design skill
description: Fewer tokens isn't less thinking. A well-structured brief and incremental tweaks get you further than re-explaining the whole project with every request.

related.title: Clint Intelligence
related.body: In practice: AI inside a CRM, with the designer defining context, limits and criteria.

blocks.text: For a long time, we learned that explaining better meant explaining more.
With AI, that logic starts to change.
Today, a designer can spend minutes writing a huge prompt, get a bad result and then spend even more time trying to fix what happened.
Maybe the problem isn't a lack of information.
Maybe it's too much information without structure.
Fewer tokens doesn't mean less thinking
There's an important difference between writing less and thinking less.
A short prompt can be shallow.
But it can also be extremely precise.
What matters isn't simply the amount of text you send to the model.
It's the amount of useful information per instruction.

data.shortP: Create a modern landing page for a tech company.
data.longP: Create a landing page for a B2B financial management SaaS. The goal is to generate demo requests. The audience is finance managers at small businesses. Prioritize value proposition, social proof and CTA. Use desktop-first, a modular structure and direct language. Don't use gradients, generic illustrations or too many decorative elements.
notes: But every piece of information removes an unnecessary possibility.

blocks.text: Prompting is also economics
Tokens, credits, context, calls, processing time and number of iterations are becoming part of the workflow.
That changes something important:
prompting can also be a matter of efficiency.
Building a good first request and then working with smaller tweaks can be more efficient than re-explaining the whole project with every interaction.
A good designer already tries to reduce friction for the user.
Now they need to start reducing friction in their own interaction with AI.
The problem with the prompt that tries to do everything

data.overloaded: Create the complete product, with onboarding, dashboard, settings, profile, notifications, payments, responsiveness, animations, accessibility, dark mode, component system...
outro: But maybe that's exactly the problem.
You're trying to resolve too many decisions at once.

steps.title: 1. Define the structure
steps.prompt: "Create the main architecture of the product."

close: That turns the conversation into a sequence of decisions.
Instead of trying to build everything at once.

blocks.caption: Re-explaining everything with each request repeats the same cost; with a good brief, the following requests only describe what changed.

blocks.text: The first prompt is the brief
The first prompt can work as a kind of brief, and the following prompts as incremental changes.
The first prompt establishes:
what we're building
The following ones define:
what changed
This logic is very similar to working on a product.
You shouldn't redefine the whole product every time you change a button.
You define the foundation and then work with controlled changes.
The question the designer should ask
Before writing:
What do I want to ask the AI?
Maybe it's better to ask:
What decision do I need to make right now?
If the decision is about architecture, we don't need to ask for a final interface.
If the decision is about navigation, we don't need to generate the whole product.
If the decision is about visual hierarchy, we don't need to rebuild every feature.
AI can speed up the process a lot.
But it can also speed up the production of things that shouldn't exist yet.
That's why spending fewer tokens isn't simply about saving money.
It can be a consequence of thinking better.

blocks.caption: Clarity reduces waste: each step discards possibilities until one solution is left.
